cells.tense: The whole pattern is in view, and it is being lived from inside it.
cells.act: step back far enough to see the whole arrangement
cells.ask: Take a step back from an arrangement you're inside of — the work, the household — and stay there long enough to see how the parts sit together. No fixing. Just let the shape show itself. No clock on it.
cells.core:
You can see the whole shape of something and still be standing in the middle of it. Most people get one or the other — lost in the middle, or so far out they've lost the feel of it. You've got both, and what you've made is showing itself as a fact you can look at, not a claim you're making.

The work is keeping the shape in sight while it keeps moving. Step back from an arrangement you're part of, long enough to see how the parts sit together. That habit keeps the hands honest. When the whole thing is in view, you don't get caught by one corner of it.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the whole thing while you're still inside it.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole arrangement

cells.tense: A future version of you is already doing the thing you haven't done yet.
cells.act: meet the thing before you know what it is
cells.ask: Take something you're sure you've got figured out — a routine, a person, a problem — and spend a few minutes with it uncategorized. Not deciding anything. Let it stay unfamiliar while you look.
cells.core:
You've seen how it goes, so you're already ahead of it — the arc, the ending, the whole shape running before the thing has arrived. That foresight is real, and it's also keeping you from being here for it. When the pattern is this clear, what's actually happening looks like something already handled, and the moment gets less of you than it's owed.

Under the predicting there's still a plain thing: this, now, before it's named. Meet it without the label. Bring something you assume you know and look at it as though you didn't. The pattern comes back when you stop aiming it forward.
cells.sheetLine: You know how it goes, so you're missing what it is.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole arrangement

cells.tense: A shape you already traced is one you no longer stand beside.
cells.act: choose this, not that, and mean it
cells.ask: Two things have been held open together. Pick the one to keep and set the other down this week. Then stay with the one you kept.
cells.core:
There's a way of working that fits you when it's going well: you trace how a thing holds together, and then you stand on what you traced. You say plainly that you know it, and act like someone who does. Seeing a system from outside while you're still in it — that part is intact, and it's yours.

What's short right now is direction. Two things want your attention and you've kept both open, refusing to let either one count. The tracing is finished. It's waiting for a hand on it — one pick, this week, and the staying-with-it that follows.
cells.sheetLine: You saw it. You just stopped standing where you saw it from.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole arrangement

cells.tense: Something is arriving right now that you are already meeting — it has simply gone unnamed.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: For a stretch of today, take what's happening in this hour before reaching for the next. When you notice yourself moving past it, that noticing is the practice. Nothing to add.
cells.core:
You're steering without your hand on it. The pattern-reading runs — how things fit, what's coming, what's needed — and it moves through you like breath you didn't decide to take. The turn is yours each time, but you haven't been putting your name on it. Nothing's lost. It works. You're just not standing where it's being run from.

What's entering now is what matters — this hour, not the shape of it. Let this moment be a fresh entry rather than a continuation of the last. When you catch yourself reaching past today, stop and take what's actually here. That's the author back beside the act.
cells.sheetLine: Something is turning here, and your name isn't on it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that this person is actually shining or dimming in front of others — the record supports a capacity for whole-pattern sight, not a fact about how visible they are. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not shining, I just notice things; that's what I do.' The asks all survive being wrong — tracing one pattern, meeting a thing unlabelled, saying this-not-that, opening the next thing — each teaches something about Recognition regardless. The sentence that serves me too much: the Too Little core's line that others see their light; cut the claim about who else sees it and keep only what the person may not be doing with what they've already found.
